newsitem.title: USA: Mars deployment back on track as problem solved.
newsitem.headline: Mars deployment back on track as problem solved.

text.p: Space officials prepared on Saturday to deploy a buggy to explore the surface of Mars after resolving a communications problem that threatened to hinder the Pathfinder mission.
Whoops of joy echoed around mission control with the word that signals had been received from the six-wheeled rover craft via the lander vehicle.
"This is fantastic news, I feel like we have been invited back to the party," Matt Wallace, rover system engineer, said.

He said the problem with the communications was in the software and had been resolved by re-cycling the modem between the rover, "Sojourner," and the lander. He likened the process to re-booting a computer.
The news ended 12 hours of nailbiting tension at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory as space engineers and techicians worked to salvage the $266 million mission.
Pathfinder crash-landed on the fourth rock from the sun on Friday after a journey of 309 million miles (497 million km) since being launched from Cape Canaveral last December 4.
The mission marked the beginning of an ambitious U.S. programme over the next decade to explore Mars and determine if it ever supported any life forms.
Sojourner cannot communicate directly with Earth. Rather, its signals must go through the lander and if the problem had not been solved, mission control would be unable to deploy the Mars rover.
Sojourner was built to explore part of the planet's surface and analyse rock and soil samples.

If full communications were not established, the rover would carry out some nominal pre-programmed tasks, but no scientific data would be relayed back to Earth, officials of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) said.

The problem also thwarted attempts to get the rover to roll down a ramp off the lander onto the surface of the planet. The operation was held up because one of the air-bags deployed to cushion Pathfiner's landing had not fully deflated. With communications restored, the rover was expected to roll onto the Martian surface later Saturday.
The Pathfinder lander continued to send spectacular images back to Earth.
Peter Smith, head of the imaging team, explained that Pathfinder landed in the area known as Ares Vallis, about 3-4 km (2-3 miles) from a large crater.
He pointed out rocks and other objects on computer-enhanced pictures, including one peak on the horizon about 20 miles (32 km) away.
He brought laughs to the audience when he pointed out one curiously shaped image on the horizon.
"The most mysterious object looks like a couch," Smith said, joking that maybe there was a homeless person on Mars.
He said at first his colleagues thought it was the parachute that had helped bring Pathfinder through the Martian atmosphere. But that was brightly coloured, he said, and this object was not.
